The blades
How fast the air may meet the blade tips at design, relative to the blade: an efficiency target (about 1.3 is typical of airliner engines).
1.2 is the certification rule (14 CFR 33.27): a rotor must survive 120 % of its redline.
Stages come in whole numbers, so the design falls short of its limit. 0: the blades slow down to close the gap. 1: they stay at the limit and every row does lighter work.

Linking the spools copies the low-pressure knobs to both.

A stator lever

At each throttle the vanes turn until the front row meets its air at the design angle again; the chart shows what that does to both shafts' speeds.

The two-shaft engine, throttle slammed

A separate engine, not the one in Design or Fly it: the Size the blades engine at its opening settings (pressure ratios 3 and 6, designed for 1500 K at the turbine inlet while flying at 250 K, 50 kPa, Mach 0.85, on the perfect gas). Its hardware stays as designed; Flight below sets the air it flies in and how fast. The fuel moves from one throttle's steady fuel flow to the other's; the controls below cut it.

Invented, representative maps (rungs 43 and 49), each with its stall line at flow coefficient 0.55.
Each throttle is named by the turbine inlet temperature its steady point holds.
τ is the high-pressure shaft's own response time; the model has no rotor weight, so it cannot give seconds.
Above 1 the low-pressure shaft is the slower one (a heavier fan and booster).
A cabin system asks for a fixed amount of air, so at low power it is a bigger share of a smaller flow. Too much, and the engine has no steady point at all.

The aircraft's air (cabin, anti-ice) is taken where the HP compressor delivers it, and never comes back. The HP compressor moves away from its stall line at every power: its face now passes more air than the burner does. (The work the lost air would have done pushes the other way, and loses; the generator knob below is that work alone — rung 92.) The LP compressor moves TOWARD its stall line at high power and away from it below about 900 K, so on this slam the LP bleed valve has to open wider to hold the same margin, and a fixed amount costs it more than the same share (rung 90). This air costs more thrust and fuel than the LP bleed's: the HP compressor has already worked on it.

Rejoins the gas just before the HP turbine's rotor, so it still does work there.
Rejoins after the HP turbine's rotor, so only the LP turbine gets work from it.

Cooling air leaves the HP compressor and comes back at the turbines, in front of the LP turbine's choked throat. That throat must then pass more gas, so the HP turbine expands less and the HP compressor loses more work than if the air had been thrown away: both compressors move TOWARD their stall lines at high power, the LP one at every power, and blade air is worse than vane air. On this slam the LP bleed valve has to bleed several times what it bleeds for the same customer share. The thrust cost runs the other way: the air leaves through the nozzle, so it costs about a third of the thrust (rung 91). The engine was sized with no cooling.

The limits come from the year and the life (Gauntner's 1980 relation).

With the throttle holding thrust or HP speed, the burner stops where either metal reaches its limit, and the end falls short of what it holds; the table says by how much. It needs turbine cooling: uncooled, the metal allows only about 990 K.

Reads the vane and blade metal temperatures at every point of the run, from the turbine inlet temperature, the compressor's exit temperature (the cooling air) and the cooling shares above, with the NASA correlation the project uses for the Cool the turbine view (Gauntner 1980). It changes nothing in the run. Without cooling the metal is over its limit at every throttle here. Watch the peak: the slam's temperature overshoot reaches the metal while the cooling air, from a compressor that has not yet sped up, is still cooler than it will be. The metal is read as if it followed the gas instantly: a real blade lags, so the peak is an upper bound.

The same unit on both shafts, so HP and LP compare at the same kilowatts. A generator draws what the aircraft needs, so at low power it is a bigger share of a smaller turbine — too much, and the engine has no steady point at all.

Holding thrust or HP speed, each end of the move asks for what this engine gives at that throttle with the generator off, and the burner runs as hot as carrying the generator needs (rung 94). On the project's test rig, holding thrust, the hotter burner moves the LP compressor away from stall, and at mid to high power, with the generator on the LP shaft, both compressors end up further from stall than with no generator at all. Holding HP speed is not holding thrust: with the generator on the HP shaft it burns much hotter and gives MORE thrust; on the LP shaft it can run the burner cooler. Ungoverned, the fuel ramps between the two ends; a load too big for a throttle is refused in words.

The generator takes power off a shaft and no air at all: no gas path changes, only the work the compressor on that shaft gets. On the HP shaft that pushes BOTH compressors toward their stall lines at every power — the HP compressor's pressure ratio falls, and that starves the LP one too — and the LP bleed valve has to bleed much more. On the LP shaft the same power costs the compressors almost nothing in the steady state (the LP's own loss is offset by the HP's pressure rise). This is why more-electric aircraft studies take the power off the LP shaft (rung 92). The engine was sized with no generator, and the burner temperature is what you set: a real control would burn hotter to carry the load.

With no generator and the move not governed, all three are the same run: the ends sit at the throttle's burner temperatures and the fuel ramps between them.

An engine in flight cannot weigh its own thrust. Its control reads something it can measure, either the pressure ratio across the engine (turbine exit over inlet) or the fan speed (the LP shaft), and turns it into thrust with a table of steady points. The chart of thrust shows the thrust the control believes beside the thrust the engine gives. Here the pressure ratio sees the jet's push exactly (the nozzle's push depends on its pressure alone), but not the drag of the air the engine swallows. While the engine speeds up it swallows less air than the table expects, so it gives more thrust than the control believes: on the default move, at most about an eighth of the thrust change. That costs more fuel, a hotter turbine and less stall margin than reading thrust itself. The fan speed misses by more, up to about half of the change and more on a slowdown, because the fan shaft is slow to follow the fuel. While the engine slows down, both readings miss the other way. With the generator on and the table made on the engine without it, the steady ends miss too: the pressure ratio by about 1 %, the fan speed by up to a quarter of the thrust.

The governor picks the fuel that makes the shaft it reads (the HP shaft, or the fan's LP shaft) close its speed gap in this time, at every power. At least 0.04 τ at the design flight's air (longer in thinner air): faster is worked out too coarsely at this step.
Fuel = the steady fuel at the asked speed × (1 + gain × the speed gap). A fixed gain closes the gap about twice as slowly at idle as near full power on this engine: the turbine has less power to give there. At most 50 at the design flight's air, less in denser air.

The throttle now asks for its quantity all along the move, not just at the two ends: it rises in a straight line from the start's value to the end's over the move, and a governor sets the fuel to give it. The temperature limiter, the acceleration schedule, the stall floor and (with the cap on) the turbine metal still cut what the governor asks for. Thrust and burner temperature answer the fuel at once, so the governor solves for them exactly; a shaft's speed cannot jump, so for HP speed the governor needs a rule for how fast to close the gap. On this engine, holding thrust along the default half-τ move asks for about 1 900 K at the end of the move, over 500 K above where it settles: the governor needs its limiters. Where the governor asks for more fuel than the engine can burn, or less than it can run on, it is held at that edge, marked under the chart. The lean edge is the solver's search bound, not a flame-out model, and a run that sits on it is worked out less precisely.

Fuel controls
Caps the fuel per unit of compressor-exit pressure at this fraction above what the engine burns when steady (0: never above it).
The fuel is cut whenever it would push that compressor's flow coefficient below this (the stall line is 0.55).

With the stators moving, the stall line moves too. A floor on the flow coefficient stays put; one on the blade incidence (the angle the air meets the blade) moves with the stall line, by the same amount at every speed.

The schedule's and the floor's cut follows its target quickly going in and slowly letting go, as a real limiter does.
Airflow levers
The valve opens just enough to keep the low-pressure compressor's flow coefficient up to this (the stall line is 0.55), up to its widest opening above.
A real valve takes time: it chases the opening it needs and closes about two-thirds of the gap in this time.
The time above is then only for opening; this one is for closing.

Each valve is priced by one of its two speeds. The valve watching blade incidence is set by how fast it OPENS: its margin is lowest before it ever starts closing, so a slow close only holds extra air on the way down. The valve watching the flow coefficient is set by how fast it CLOSES: its margin is lowest while it is closing, so a slow close lets it run a lower target and bleed less. In the project's test grid a slow close made the flow-coefficient valve the cheaper one at every opening speed, and a fast close handed the incidence valve the slow openings too (rung 89).

A slow valve falls behind where it has to open quickly. The valve watching blade incidence waits until the margin is actually needed and then has to open fast, so a slow one loses protection there. The valve watching the flow coefficient holds more margin than it needs, and that extra absorbs the delay. Slow enough, and the flow-coefficient valve gives the same margin with less air: the reverse of the instant valve (rung 88). A slow valve cannot run beside the temperature limiter's lag or the realistic release.

With the low-pressure stators moving, a valve watching the flow coefficient fights them: it bleeds air to undo the drop in flow coefficient that the stators make on purpose. A valve watching blade incidence lets the stators do part of its job. Pair it with a stall floor that watches the same thing: beside a floor on the flow coefficient, the incidence valve lets the flow coefficient fall and the floor starves the run (rung 87). Set the floor a little below the valve: at the same number the two share the work in a way the model's rounding decides.

Each lever is back at its design setting by the design speed. Both together run beside any fuel limiter. Watch the stall floor read as a flow coefficient: the stators lower the flow coefficient, so that floor can cut the fuel from the first instant until the run stops; the bleed lifts it back.

Cool the turbine

The two-shaft engine of Controls (pressure ratios 3 and 6, designed at 1500 K, perfect gas, 250 K, 50 kPa, Mach 0.85). Its turbine's metal has a temperature limit; air from the high-pressure compressor cools it. The chart sweeps the burner temperature and shows the cooling that holds both metals exactly at their limits, and what that costs.

How much air a row needs for a given cooling job: internal convection needs twice what full-coverage film cooling does, a thermal-barrier coating 1.5 times, transpiration 0.8 times (Gauntner 1980).

The same invented maps as Controls (rungs 43 and 49); a redesigned engine runs at its own design point, where the map does not enter.

The hottest burner temperature this engine's metal allows with your cooling, and which row sets it. Vane air also cools the gas the rotor blades see, so more vane air hands the limit to the blades.

The burner of the engine you design in Design the engine (its flight and cycle knobs are below), always read on the equilibrium gas: the NO models need its chemistry. Nothing here changes the engine's thrust or fuel; NO is a trace.

A guessed number (about 3 ms is typical): read the trend, not the size.

Flight

The two-shaft engine keeps the hardware it was designed with (at Mach 0.85) and flies here in the air and at the speed set above. Flying faster rams the air denser and warmer before it reaches the compressor; flying slower does the opposite. Thinner air at the engine passes less of it through, so the shafts spin up more slowly: time stays in the spool time constant of the design flight, so the same throttle move reads slower up high or slow, and runs hotter while the shafts catch up. The throttles stay in kelvin: in colder air the same turbine temperature runs the shafts faster. The speed governor's limits scale with the density of the air the engine takes in: a smaller gain in denser air, a longer time constant in thinner. Even so, on a cold day, or where the governor sits at its rich edge in thin air, its run is somewhat rougher (up to about 0.0006 in flow coefficient against a finer step, measured; elsewhere about 0.0001). Flying very fast heats the air so much that a low throttle has no steady point (the default move is refused at Mach 3.5, runs from 1300 K; on the flat-LP map the lowest start rises from about 1000 K at Mach 1.6 to 1600 K at Mach 2.6). Flown fast at a low throttle the thrust can go below zero (Mach 3 from 1000 K: about −320 N per kg/s of design airflow): slowing the air the engine swallows costs more push than its jet gives back.

A real control's tables (the thrust it reads from the pressure ratio or the fan speed, the acceleration schedule, the speed governor's fuel) are made once, at one flight, and read everywhere else through two corrections: thrust and fuel divided by how much denser the air at the engine is, speeds by the square root of how much warmer. Here the pressure one is exact. The temperature one is nearly so: in air 16 % warmer at the engine the pressure ratio's thrust is off by under 0.1 %, the fan speed's by about 0.2 %, because the fuel's heat is fixed while the air's grows with temperature. No correction sees a change of flight speed: a table made at Mach 0.85 gives about 8 % too much thrust at Mach 0.5 and 5–10 % too little at Mach 1.4 (the jet's push against the outside air and the drag of the air swallowed both change; the engine's inside does not). Switch a correction off to see why it is there. Without the pressure one the thrust is off by about as much as the air is thinner or denser. Without the temperature one the fan-speed control misses by 22–43 % on a day 16 % warmer or 13 % colder at the engine, while the pressure ratio needs no temperature correction at all, and the schedule runs cooler in hot air and hotter in cold. The speed governor's own table, read uncorrected, runs off its end and holds the end's fuel, so it settles slow in hot air as well as cold. The acceleration schedule needs no pressure correction (fuel over compressor pressure already divides it out). Very fast flight (about Mach 2.5 and above) is beyond a design-flight table's reach: make the tables at this flight there.

The fuel follows the schedule (governed: what the governor asks for) unless a control cuts it; the cut fuel is what burns. Each control acts on its own measurement: the temperature limiter on the turbine inlet temperature, the acceleration schedule on fuel per unit of compressor pressure, the stall floor on a compressor's flow coefficient. When several are on, the one asking for the least fuel wins. The cooling that holds both metals at their limits

Burner (K)Vane air (%)Blade air (%) Thrust (N per kg/s)Uncooled thrustFuel per thrust (mg/N·s)UncooledCooling air (K)

Each point puts both metals exactly at their limits: the vanes, which see the burner's hottest gas, and the rotor blades, which see gas the vane air has already cooled. The gas each row sees includes Gauntner's hot spot and safety margin. "Uncooled" is the same engine (or the same fresh design) at the same burner temperature with no cooling at all, its metal far past the limit: it shows what the cooling costs, not an engine anyone could run. On this engine, cooling slows the high-pressure shaft and so cools its own cooling air; a fresh design's compressor delivers the same air temperature at every burner temperature. No efficiency loss from cooling is counted, and the engine's hardware was sized with no cooling.

The burner

QuantityThis burner

All the fuel burns in the front zone with part of the air; the rest of the air then dilutes it down to the turbine inlet temperature. NO forms in the hot front zone and is frozen through the dilution, so the emission index (per kilogram of fuel) is set there. "If perfectly mixed" is the same chemistry at the turbine inlet temperature: almost no NO, which is why the front zone is where it all happens. The model's anchor is the stoichiometric front zone's emission index, inside the band airliner engines certify at; every other number rests on guessed constants (marked), so read their trends.

NO against the front zone's richness

this burner's setting, sweptpinned big dot: this burner×: does not run there

Richer than 1 the front zone runs out of oxygen: its flame cools and its O atoms vanish, so NO collapses. That is why low-NO burners burn rich first (rich-quench-lean). But the rich gas must then pass stoichiometric on its way down to the turbine inlet temperature; a slow quench makes NO again on that crossing (try "Over a set time").

NO against jet strength

this burner, jet strength sweptpinned the mixing model's best jet×: does not run there

A stronger jet mixes faster. With one well-mixed stream (rung 11) that only ever helps. The mixing models add unevenness across the duct: past the best jet the air overshoots and leaves rich, hot pockets, and NO can turn back up.

The sized blades

QuantityLow-pressureHigh-pressure

Two limits set each spool's design blade speed: the airflow level (an efficiency target) and the blade material (the root of an untapered blade at its yield strength, brought down by the overspeed factor). The slower one wins. The stage count follows from the work the spool must do at that speed, rounded up to whole rows. The redline is the speed at which the blade root reaches its strength limit, divided by the overspeed factor.

Speeds are physical shaft speeds against design. The vane angle includes the design pre-swirl; rung 85's crossings sit near 66–69°, further than real vanes turn. "Never reached" rows are read at the last setting the search reached; along the way the other shaft can run faster than at that end (it did, mid-way, in a third of such cases sampled, never above its redline). The strength limit is optimistic (no taper, no disc, no hot-metal weakening, yield rather than breaking strength), so "crosses" is robust and "under" is one-sided. On the thermally perfect gas, the row-by-row levers still split the pressure rise between rows with a fixed γ of 1.4.

Slam the throttle

QuantityTemperature commandedFuel metered

Temperature commanded makes the turbine-inlet temperature follow the move exactly, as textbooks do. Fuel metered moves the fuel flow instead, between the two steady fuel flows; the temperature is then whatever the burner gives. On a slam the shaft cannot yet pump the extra air, so the temperature overshoots. A real engine meters fuel. The map below shows each run's path; on a slam it swings toward the stall line. The stall margin tile reads the steady point only while the nozzle is choked (rung 36); here the flow coefficient itself is shown at every moment, beside the stall line you set, and the stretches where the nozzle is unchoked are drawn thin and dashed.

Performance

QuantityValue

What is computed, and what is not. Each change runs the project's design-point cycle (build_turbojet(…).run(…), the same call the command line makes) for the gas model you pick: one engine with its compressor sized to your pressure ratio and its burner to your turbine inlet temperature. It is a design point, not a fixed engine being throttled. Flight altitude and air temperature/pressure are linked through the 1976 US Standard Atmosphere: type a pressure and the altitude becomes the pressure altitude. Type a temperature and the "off standard day" value follows. Above Mach 1 the inlet loses extra pressure through the model's supersonic recovery law.

The T–s diagram. Stations 0 and 9 are the still outside air and the exhaust jet (static states). Stations 2–5 are total (stagnation) states. Entropy is measured from the outside air. The air and the burned gas are different mixtures, so the jump across the burner mixes heat added with that change of mixture. The burner and the exhaust-cooling legs are drawn as curves: the shape is the burned gas's own constant-pressure line, and whatever that misses the next station by (the pressure loss, the change of mixture) is spread evenly along the way, so the curves meet the station points exactly. With the perfect gas, the textbook constants (cp = 1004, R = 287, γ = 1.4) do not quite agree with each other. An ideal compressor then shows a tiny, exactly predictable slope instead of a vertical line.

Fly it. The design's hardware is frozen: the turbine and nozzle throat areas, and the flow and speed it was designed for. Moving the throttle or the flight then lets the engine find its own pressure ratio, airflow and shaft speed (the project's rungs 31–36: a choked turbine, a fixed convergent nozzle that may unchoke at low power, and a representative compressor map). Capturing a throat area needs a convergent nozzle, so the frozen design is re-run with one; its numbers can differ from a "fully expanded" design. The exhaust pushes against the air pressure of the flight you set. The stall margin is rung 36's: it rests on a stall line you choose and a map shape you pick, so only its trend (thinner at low power) is meaningful. It is not modelled while the nozzle is unchoked.

Slam the throttle. The project's rungs 34 and 35: the shaft speed becomes something that changes in time, driven by the gap between the turbine's power and the compressor's, and the engine is stepped forward in small time steps. Time is counted in the shaft's own response time τ (its rotor inertia times the design speed squared, over the design shaft power); the model has no rotor inertia, so it cannot give seconds, and its findings are about how long the move takes compared with τ. A move must last a whole number of the model's 0.02 τ steps: one that ends between steps makes the peak temperature depend on the step size. When a run cannot continue, the page shows the points it has and why it stopped (some stops are limits of the model, said as such). The equilibrium gas is not offered here: the model cannot meter fuel on it.

Size the blades. Rung 85 on its own two-spool engine (a separate engine from Design's, which has one compressor). Each compressor's front row is sized from two limits, how fast the air may meet the blade tips (an efficiency target) and the blade material's strength at the root, and the stage count, blade speeds and the redline come out. A stator lever then holds the front row's design angle as the throttle comes back, and the chart shows whether either shaft passes its redline. The two-spool model only handles a choked nozzle; throttles where it unchokes are listed as not modelled.

Controls. The project's rungs 43–62 and 86 on the two-shaft engine of Size the blades: both shaft speeds change in time, the fuel is metered and the turbine temperature is an output (it overshoots on a slam), and the fuel controls a real engine carries can be switched on, each with its one number: a turbine temperature limiter and its reaction lag, an acceleration schedule read off the engine's own steady running line, a stall floor on either compressor, and a realistic fast-in, slow-out lag on the schedule and the floor. Airflow levers can be added: variable stators, a bleed valve, or both together (rung 86), each scheduled on shaft speed. Each run is the model's own march, step for step. A run that stops early shows the points it has and why, by kind: the floor could no longer be held by any fuel cut; the model's every-step check at the full scheduled fuel had no answer while a limiter held the fuel far below it (a limit of the model's method); the mixture became leaner or richer than the model's fuel solver searches (0.004 and 0.065 kg of fuel per kg of air). With the temperature limiter's lag on, the model does not record the lag's state, so a stop there is reported without a cause. Time is in the high-pressure shaft's response time τ; the bleed thrust counts the dumped air's full ram drag. The engine can be flown at another altitude, air temperature and Mach number: its hardware stays as designed, every steady point and the march itself are worked out in the new flight, and τ stays the design flight's, so where the engine takes in thinner air the same move reads slower. There is no Reynolds-number effect: in the model a component's efficiency does not fall in thin air, as a real one's does. At low throttles in dense or warm air, or flying slowly, the nozzle unchokes: it then passes less gas at a given pressure, and the low-pressure turbine expands only as far as still leaves the nozzle enough pressure to push the gas out (rung 97; both turbines' inlet guide vanes stay choked, as modelled throughout). Those stretches are drawn thin and dashed.

Burner. The project's rungs 7–24, beside the cycle: they never change a cycle number. They read four numbers off the Design engine run on the equilibrium gas (compressor exit temperature, turbine inlet temperature, fuel-air ratio, burner pressure) and do their own chemistry: an equilibrium flame in the front zone, the extended Zeldovich reactions for NO over the time the gas stays there, and the dilution down to the turbine inlet temperature, instantly, over a set time, or through jets with one of the eight mixing models. The grids the models integrate on are fixed, coarser than the command line's (within about 1 % of it, every best jet in place; measured). Most constants are the model's own guesses and are marked so: read trends, not sizes. The anchor is rung 8's: a stoichiometric front zone at this design gives an emission index inside the band airliner engines certify at. The nozzle readout is rung 14's frozen-against-re-reacting expansion, carrying the burner's NO; with a mixing model that NO is converted from its emission index the way rung 17 does.

Cool the turbine. The project's rung 93 on the two-shaft engine of Controls: the turbine's vanes and rotor blades each have a metal temperature limit, set from a material year and a part life by Gauntner's 1980 NASA relation, and the air from the high-pressure compressor that cools them (rung 91's vane and blade air) is sized by Gauntner's correlation: a row needs more air the hotter the gas it sees and the colder the metal must stay, scaled by the cooling technology. The sweep finds, at each burner temperature, the cooling that holds both metals exactly at their limits, on this engine run hotter or on an engine redesigned at that temperature. The knob form takes your cooling and finds the hottest burner temperature the metal allows on this engine. The correlation is a fit to engines of its time: read the trends and the comparisons, not the last kelvin.

Efficiencies. Overall efficiency is thrust power per fuel power. The model splits it into a thermal and a propulsive part using the jet's speed alone. When the jet leaves the nozzle above the outside pressure (a fixed convergent nozzle, especially high up), part of the thrust is that pressure push, which the speed-based split does not count, so the propulsive part can read above 100 %. It can also near zero thrust (around idle): the jet then barely outruns the flight, and the fuel's own mass, which the model counts as accelerated, dominates both the thrust and the energy gain. The overall figure is unaffected.

Numbers computed here agree with the command-line model to the last few digits. The browser uses a different maths library, and the project's test run checks that difference stays below a measured bound.
